newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia government makes windfall from airports.
newsitem.headline: Australia government makes windfall from airports.

text.p: Australia completed the first phase of its airport privatisation plan on Wednesday with the sale of three city airports for A$3.34 billion (US$2.60 billion) -- more than twice the amount the government had budgeted for.
Analysts said the government had assumed it would get only about A$1.5 billion for 50-year leases on Brisbane, Melbourne and Perth airports, among the largest of 20 airports to be sold.
The sale also cleared the way for the second phase of airport privatisation -- the sale of all remaining airports except those in Sydney in the 1997/98 year starting on July 1.

Melbourne airport was sold for A$1.307 billion to Australian Pacific Airports Corp (APAC), a consortium led by funds manager Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) and British airports operator BAA Plc.
Brisbane airport was awarded to a group headed by Dutch government-owned Amsterdam Airport Schiphol and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia Ltd for A$1.387 billion.

Perth airport was sold for A$643 million to Airstralia Development Group Pty Ltd, a consortium including Lockheed Martin Corp subsidiary Airport Group Holdings International, Hastings Funds Management and an infrastructure subsidiary of HRL Morrison & Co.
Australian Finance Minister John Fahey confirmed the amounts were more than expected, but refused to say by how much.
"The prices we received are considerably higher than we anticipated might have been received before we started this process," Fahey told reporters.
The airport selloff came only a week after Australia's largest single privatisation, the A$4.86-billion sale to U.S. utilities of a power station and coalmine in Victoria state.
Fahey said the government would move to sell its remaining airports, apart from those in Sydney, in the fiscal year to June 30, 1998.
"We would hope to move early in the financial year in respect of the others and we will look at that," he said.
"There is some considerable interest in acquiring a number of those airports."

Transport Minister John Sharp said he was unable to pinpoint an exact time for the sale of Sydney's Mascot airport or the planned second airport, adding that Mascot would not be sold until its aircraft noise problems were satisfactorily solved.
"It will be some time before we've reached that situation and so we will not be making a decision about Sydney airport for some time to come," Sharp told reporters.
Sharp said the successful tenderers for the first three airports had indicated they would spend about A$500 million on the airports to improve their services over the next 10 years.
Landing charges -- and therefore, airfares -- would also come down as the consortiums had agreed to comply with the government's recently-revamped pricing regime.
APAC said it would provide A$345 million in equity for its purchase of Melbourne airport and borrow the rest.
AMP holds a 49.9-percent stake in the consortium and Sydney-based funds manager Axoim has 25 percent, while BAA Plc would have an initial stake of 25.1 percent.
Its stake would fall to 15.1 percent if a proposed fourth partner, Melbourne-based Hastings Funds Management, exercised an option to take a 10 percent stake.
The Airstralia Development Group consortium is owned 49 percent by Infratil Australia Trust, 16 percent by Airports Group International Ltd, and 35 percent by Australian Airport Property Fund.
